blocks.body:
The symmetric group $S_3$ acts on $\mathbb{C}^3$ by permuting coordinates. Two subspaces are left alone by every permutation: the line $L$ spanned by $(1,1,1)$ and the plane $P = \{x + y + z = 0\}$. Since $\mathbb{C}^3 = L \oplus P$, the action splits into a $1$-dimensional piece where $S_3$ does nothing and a $2$-dimensional piece which, as we will check, cannot be split any further.

Representation theory studies a group through the ways it can act by linear maps, and asks this question in general: can every linear action of a finite group be cut into indivisible pieces, and what are the pieces? For finite groups over $\mathbb{C}$ the answer is a clean yes (Maschke's theorem), and the pieces obey strong rules (Schur's lemma). Linear algebra then gives information about the group, and the group gives information about linear problems with symmetry, from vibrating molecules to Fourier analysis. The page uses [[group-actions]] and [[inner-products]].

blocks.title: Representation
blocks.body:
A representation of a group $G$ on a finite-dimensional complex vector space $V$ is a group homomorphism
$$\rho\colon G \to \mathrm{GL}(V), \qquad \rho(gh) = \rho(g)\rho(h).$$
The dimension of $V$ is the degree of $\rho$. A subspace $W \subseteq V$ is invariant (a subrepresentation) if $\rho(g)W \subseteq W$ for all $g$. A representation $V \neq 0$ is irreducible if its only invariant subspaces are $0$ and $V$. Two representations $(\rho, V)$ and $(\sigma, W)$ are equivalent (isomorphic) if there is a linear isomorphism $T\colon V \to W$ with $T\rho(g) = \sigma(g)T$ for all $g$; more generally a linear map with this property is called a $G$-map or intertwiner.

Choosing a basis turns a representation into a homomorphism into invertible $n \times n$ matrices; equivalent representations are the same up to a change of basis.

blocks.title: First examples
blocks.body:
- The trivial representation: $V = \mathbb{C}$ and $\rho(g) = 1$ for all $g$.
- The sign representation of $S_n$: $\rho(\sigma) = \mathrm{sgn}(\sigma) = \pm 1$ on $\mathbb{C}$.
- The cyclic group $\mathbb{Z}/n$ on $\mathbb{C}$: $\rho_j(k) = \omega^{jk}$ where $\omega = e^{2\pi i/n}$ and $j$ is fixed. This is a homomorphism because $\omega^n = 1$.
- Permutation representations: if $G$ acts on a finite set $X$, let $\mathbb{C}^X$ have basis vectors $e_x$ for $x \in X$ and put $\rho(g) e_x = e_{g x}$. Each $\rho(g)$ is a permutation matrix. The opening example is $S_3$ acting on $X = \{1,2,3\}$.
- The regular representation: the permutation representation of $G$ acting on itself by left multiplication, of degree $|G|$.
- Geometric representations: the dihedral group of the square acts on $\mathbb{R}^2$ (or $\mathbb{C}^2$) by rotations and reflections; $\mathbb{Z}/4$ acts by rotation through multiples of $90^\circ$.

Every $1$-dimensional representation is irreducible. A degree-$1$ representation is just a homomorphism $G \to \mathbb{C}^\times$, and since $\rho(g)^{|G|} = \rho(g^{|G|}) = 1$, its values are roots of unity.

blocks.title: Example 1: the 2-dimensional representation of S3
blocks.body: Show that the plane $P = \{(x,y,z) : x + y + z = 0\}$ inside the permutation representation of $S_3$ on $\mathbb{C}^3$ is irreducible.
blocks.solution:
$P$ is invariant because permuting coordinates does not change their sum. A proper nonzero invariant subspace of the $2$-dimensional space $P$ would be a line $\mathbb{C}v$ fixed by every $\rho(\sigma)$, so $v$ would be a common eigenvector of all the permutation matrices.

Let $t = (1\,2)$ swap the first two coordinates. On $P$ it has the eigenvector $u_1 = (1,-1,0)$ with eigenvalue $-1$ and $u_2 = (1,1,-2)$ with eigenvalue $+1$. These eigenvalues are distinct, so every eigenvector of $\rho(t)$ in $P$ is a multiple of $u_1$ or of $u_2$. Now let $s = (2\,3)$ swap the last two coordinates: $\rho(s)u_1 = (1,0,-1)$ and $\rho(s)u_2 = (1,-2,1)$, neither of which is a multiple of the vector it came from. So there is no common eigenvector, and $P$ is irreducible.

Thus $\mathbb{C}^3 = L \oplus P$ is a decomposition into irreducibles: the trivial representation plus a $2$-dimensional irreducible one, often called the standard representation of $S_3$.

blocks.title: When decomposition fails
blocks.body:
Not every representation splits into irreducibles, and the counterexamples show what the hypotheses of the main theorem are for.

The infinite group $\mathbb{Z}$ acts on $\mathbb{C}^2$ by $n \mapsto \begin{pmatrix} 1 & n \\ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix}$. The line spanned by $e_1$ is invariant, and it is the only invariant line, because the only eigenvectors of $\begin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix}$ are multiples of $e_1$. So it has no invariant complement, and $\mathbb{C}^2$ is not a direct sum of irreducibles.

The same matrices with entries in the field $\mathbb{F}_p$ give a representation of the finite group $\mathbb{Z}/p$ on $\mathbb{F}_p^2$ (the matrix with $n = p$ is the identity mod $p$), and the same argument shows it does not split. Here the problem is that the characteristic $p$ divides $|G| = p$.

So two things matter: the group should be finite, and the field should have characteristic not dividing $|G|$. Over $\mathbb{C}$ the second condition is automatic. The key tool is averaging over the group, which needs division by $|G|$.

blocks.title: Maschke's theorem
blocks.body:
Let $G$ be a finite group and $V$ a finite-dimensional complex representation of $G$. Then every invariant subspace $W \subseteq V$ has an invariant complement $W'$, with $V = W \oplus W'$. Consequently $V$ is a direct sum of irreducible representations,
$$V = V_1 \oplus V_2 \oplus \cdots \oplus V_r .$$
The same holds over any field whose characteristic does not divide $|G|$.

Start with any inner product $\langle \cdot, \cdot \rangle$ on $V$ and average it over the group:
$$\langle u, v \rangle_G = \frac{1}{|G|} \sum_{g \in G} \langle \rho(g)u, \rho(g)v \rangle .$$
This is again an inner product: it is linear in the first variable, conjugate-symmetric, and $\langle v, v\rangle_G$ is an average of positive numbers when $v \ne 0$. It is also $G$-invariant. For $h \in G$,
$$\langle \rho(h)u, \rho(h)v \rangle_G = \frac{1}{|G|}\sum_{g \in G} \langle \rho(gh)u, \rho(gh)v \rangle = \langle u, v \rangle_G ,$$
because $g \mapsto gh$ is a bijection of $G$, so the sum is merely reordered.

Let $W' = W^\perp$ be the orthogonal complement with respect to $\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle_G$; then $V = W \oplus W'$. To see that $W'$ is invariant, take $v \in W'$, $g \in G$, $w \in W$. By invariance of the inner product,
$$\langle \rho(g)v, w \rangle_G = \langle \rho(g^{-1})\rho(g)v, \rho(g^{-1})w \rangle_G = \langle v, \rho(g^{-1})w \rangle_G = 0,$$
since $\rho(g^{-1})w \in W$. So $\rho(g)v \in W'$.

For the consequence, induct on $\dim V$. If $V$ is irreducible we are done. Otherwise pick an invariant $W$ with $0 \ne W \ne V$, write $V = W \oplus W'$, and decompose $W$ and $W'$, both of smaller dimension.

Over a field $k$ with $\mathrm{char}\, k \nmid |G|$ there may be no inner product, but the same averaging works for projections: if $\pi\colon V \to W$ is any linear projection onto $W$, then $\pi^\circ = \frac{1}{|G|}\sum_g \rho(g)\pi\rho(g)^{-1}$ is still a projection onto $W$, it commutes with every $\rho(h)$, and its kernel is an invariant complement.

blocks.title: Unitarity and the averaging projection
blocks.body:
The proof gives more: in the averaged inner product every $\rho(g)$ preserves lengths, so it is a unitary operator. By [[spectral-theorem|the spectral theorem]] each $\rho(g)$ is diagonalisable with eigenvalues of absolute value $1$, and since $\rho(g)^{|G|} = I$ these eigenvalues are roots of unity. Every complex representation of a finite group can be written, in a suitable basis, with unitary matrices.

The same averaging idea gives a formula that is useful by itself. Let $V^G = \{v : \rho(g)v = v \text{ for all } g\}$ be the subspace of fixed vectors, and set
$$P = \frac{1}{|G|}\sum_{g \in G} \rho(g).$$
For any $h$, $\rho(h)P = P$ (reindex the sum), so every vector $Pv$ is fixed; and if $v$ is fixed then $Pv = v$. Hence $P$ is a projection onto $V^G$, so $P^2 = P$, and the trace of a projection equals its rank:
$$\dim V^G = \operatorname{tr} P = \frac{1}{|G|}\sum_{g \in G} \operatorname{tr} \rho(g).$$

blocks.title: Example 2: counting orbits with the averaging formula
blocks.body: How many ways are there to colour the $6$ beads of a necklace black or white, if two colourings that differ by a rotation are considered the same?
blocks.solution:
Let $X$ be the set of $2^6 = 64$ colourings, with $G = \mathbb{Z}/6$ acting by rotation, and take the permutation representation $\mathbb{C}^X$. A vector $\sum c_x e_x$ is fixed by $G$ exactly when $c$ is constant on each orbit, so $\dim (\mathbb{C}^X)^G$ is the number of orbits, which is what we want. And $\operatorname{tr}\rho(g)$ is the trace of a permutation matrix, which is the number of colourings fixed by $g$. The formula above becomes Burnside's counting lemma: the number of orbits is the average number of fixed points.

A rotation by $k$ steps splits the $6$ positions into $\gcd(k,6)$ cycles, and a colouring is fixed exactly when it is constant on each cycle, so it fixes $2^{\gcd(k,6)}$ colourings. For $k = 0,1,2,3,4,5$ this gives $64, 2, 4, 8, 4, 2$, with sum $84$. The answer is $84/6 = 14$ necklaces.

blocks.title: Schur's lemma
blocks.body:
Let $V$ and $W$ be irreducible representations of $G$ and $T\colon V \to W$ a $G$-map.

1. Either $T = 0$ or $T$ is an isomorphism.
2. If $V = W$ is a complex representation, then $T = \lambda I$ for some $\lambda \in \mathbb{C}$.

1. The kernel of $T$ is invariant: if $Tv = 0$ then $T\rho(g)v = \sigma(g)Tv = 0$. Since $V$ is irreducible, $\ker T$ is $0$ or $V$. Similarly the image of $T$ is an invariant subspace of $W$, so it is $0$ or $W$. If $T \ne 0$ then $\ker T = 0$ and $\operatorname{im} T = W$, so $T$ is an isomorphism.

2. As $\mathbb{C}$ is algebraically closed and $V$ is finite-dimensional, $T$ has an eigenvalue $\lambda$. Then $T - \lambda I$ is also a $G$-map, and it is not injective. By part 1 it is zero, so $T = \lambda I$.

blocks.title: Abelian groups
blocks.body:
Schur's lemma has an immediate consequence for abelian groups. If $G$ is abelian and $V$ is irreducible, then each $\rho(h)$ commutes with every $\rho(g)$, so $\rho(h)$ is a $G$-map and therefore a scalar. But then every subspace of $V$ is invariant, and irreducibility forces $\dim V = 1$. Every irreducible complex representation of a finite abelian group is $1$-dimensional.

For $G = \mathbb{Z}/n$ this means: a representation is the same as one invertible matrix $A = \rho(1)$ with $A^n = I$, and Maschke's theorem says $A$ can be diagonalised, with eigenvalues among the $n$-th roots of unity. The irreducible representations are the $n$ characters $\rho_j(k) = \omega^{jk}$ for $j = 0, \dots, n-1$, and decomposing a representation of $\mathbb{Z}/n$ into them is the same as the discrete Fourier transform.

The field matters. The rotation representation of $\mathbb{Z}/4$ on $\mathbb{R}^2$ is irreducible over $\mathbb{R}$ (no real line is fixed by a $90^\circ$ rotation), but over $\mathbb{C}$ it splits, as the next example shows.

blocks.title: Example 3: rotations of the plane over C
blocks.body: Let $\mathbb{Z}/4$ act on $\mathbb{C}^2$ by $\rho(k) = R^k$ with $R = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & -1 \\ 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix}$ (rotation by $90^\circ$). Decompose it into irreducibles.
blocks.solution:
The characteristic polynomial of $R$ is $\lambda^2 + 1$, with roots $\pm i$. Eigenvectors: $R(1, -i)^{\mathsf T} = (i, 1)^{\mathsf T} = i\,(1,-i)^{\mathsf T}$ and $R(1, i)^{\mathsf T} = (-i, 1)^{\mathsf T} = -i\,(1, i)^{\mathsf T}$. The two eigenlines are invariant under every power of $R$, so
$$\mathbb{C}^2 = \mathbb{C}(1,-i) \oplus \mathbb{C}(1,i) \cong \rho_1 \oplus \rho_3,$$
where $\rho_j(k) = i^{jk}$: on the first line $k$ acts by $i^k$, on the second by $(-i)^k = i^{3k}$. Over $\mathbb{R}$ no such decomposition exists, because $R$ has no real eigenvalue.

blocks.title: Where this leads
blocks.body:
Maschke's theorem says every representation is built from irreducibles; the next questions are how many irreducibles a group has and how big they are. The answers, proved on the page on [[character-theory]], are remarkably rigid. A finite group has only finitely many irreducible representations up to equivalence, say $V_1, \dots, V_k$; their number $k$ equals the number of conjugacy classes of $G$; each $V_i$ appears in the regular representation exactly $\dim V_i$ times; and so
$$\sum_{i=1}^{k} (\dim V_i)^2 = |G|.$$
For $S_3$ there are three conjugacy classes and three irreducibles: trivial, sign and the $2$-dimensional one of Example 1, and indeed $1 + 1 + 4 = 6$. Moreover the multiplicity of each $V_i$ in any representation is determined, even though the subspaces themselves may not be.

Two further constructions are used constantly. If $V$, $W$ are representations, so are $V \oplus W$, the tensor product $V \otimes W$ with $g$ acting by $\rho(g) \otimes \sigma(g)$ (see [[tensor-products]]), and the dual $V^*$. And a representation of $G$ on $V$ is the same thing as a module over the group algebra $\mathbb{C}[G]$, so the theory is a chapter of the theory of [[modules]]; in this language Maschke's theorem says that $\mathbb{C}[G]$ is a semisimple ring.

- Maschke's theorem needs a finite group (or, later, a compact one) and a field of characteristic not dividing $|G|$. The two counterexamples above show that neither hypothesis can be dropped.
- The decomposition into irreducibles is unique only up to isomorphism and reordering, not as a set of subspaces. In $\mathbb{C}^2$ with $G$ acting trivially, every line is an invariant subspace, and any two distinct lines give a decomposition.
- An invariant subspace is not the same as a subspace of fixed vectors: the plane $P$ in Example 1 is invariant, yet $S_3$ fixes no nonzero vector in it.
- Equivalent representations can look very different as matrices; to compare them, use a basis-free invariant such as the character.

Characters, the traces of representations, turn all of this into computation; see [[character-theory]]. The irreducible representations of $\mathbb{Z}/n$ are the exponentials of the discrete Fourier transform, and for the circle group the analogous decomposition of functions is the theory of [[fourier-series]]. For compact groups such as rotation groups the average over $G$ is replaced by an integral, and the theory continues on [[lie-groups]] and [[lie-algebras]]. In quantum mechanics, the states of a system with symmetry group $G$ form a representation of $G$, and the decomposition into irreducibles explains the degeneracies of energy levels. Representations are also the functors from a one-object category to vector spaces; see [[categories-functors]].

1. Show that every $1$-dimensional representation of $S_n$ is either trivial or the sign. (Hint: transpositions are all conjugate.)
2. Decompose the permutation representation of $\mathbb{Z}/3$ on $\mathbb{C}^3$ (cyclic shift of coordinates) into three $1$-dimensional representations, giving an eigenvector for each.
3. Show that the representation of $\mathbb{Z}/p$ on $\mathbb{F}_p^2$ given by $k \mapsto \begin{pmatrix} 1 & k \\ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix}$ has exactly one invariant line.
4. Use the averaging formula to count the colourings of the four cells of a $2 \times 2$ board with three colours, up to rotation of the board.
